cim: Michigan tapping artificial intelligence to address prison violence
cim_eredeti: Michigan tapping artificial intelligence to address prison violence
szoveg_eredeti:
LANSING — The Michigan Department of Corrections is tapping artificial intelligence in a bid to more safely house the state's 32,000 inmates amid a rise in prison violence, including at least four recent incidents in which inmates are suspected of killing their cellmates.

The plan would use an AI-based system to rank the security risk of inmates from Level 1, the lowest risk, to Level 5, the highest risk, based on numerous factors including the nature of their crimes, assessments by department experts, and how they have behaved in prisons. Currently, such classifications, which give each inmate a numerical score, are done manually using worksheets. The new system would be largely automated and update each inmate's information and security classification in real time, according to an Oct. 28 news release from the Michigan Department of Corrections.

But the president of the union representing Michigan corrections officers is skeptical about the new approach. The problem, said Byron Osborn, isn't that the security classifications prison officials now calculate without the use of AI are inaccurate. The problem is that the MDOC has too few of the highest-security prison beds – Level 4 and Level 5 – to house the inmates deemed to be highest risk, Osborn said.

Level 4 inmates are housed together in two-person cells, where there have been three recent homicides at Bellamy Creek Correctional Facility in Ionia and one at Carson City Correctional Facility. Level 5 inmates are housed in single-person cells and have further restrictions on their movements. Level 1 and Level 2 inmates are housed in dorm-like settings and have greater freedom of movement and more programming options. There is no Level 3.

Michigan prisons saw a 13% increase in assaults on staff and inmates between 2019 and 2026, despite a 16% drop in the prison population during that period, according to reports filed with the Michigan Legislature. Corrections officers tie much of the violence to a chronic staff shortage that results in more lockdowns for inmates, heightening their frustration levels, and insufficient staff to manage situations before they escalate. They also blame a lack of Level 4 and Level 5 beds, which are costlier because they require higher staffing levels. Inmates who should be housed alone in Level 5 are sharing cells with other inmates, and inmates who should be in Level 4 are being housed in Level 1 and Level 2, officers say.

Department Director Heidi Washington said in an Oct. 28 news release that using the new AI tool "is expected to improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30%, improving safety for staff and those who are incarcerated."

The MDOC hired Recidiviz, a Utah-based nonprofit technology organization, to help develop the new system that will be introduced as a pilot project at selected prisons starting Dec. 1, according to the news release.

The MDOC and the Department of Technology, Management and Budget signed a $1 million contract with Recvidiviz in 2021 to build a "criminal justice data platform," state records show. That contract has since been extended three times and is now valued at just over $4 million, according to state records. An MDOC spokesperson did not immediately respond Oct. 29 to an email asking whether, and to what extent, the criminal justice data platform includes more functions than the prison classification system.

“Classifying prisoners at the security level that fits their current behaviors and needs keeps everyone safer – the individual, other incarcerated people, and correctional staff," Washington said.

Osborn said he is glad the MDOC has acknowledged there is a problem but the planned pilot project was announced without prior consultation with corrections officers and does not appear to address the major problem.

If the new system provides more accurate classification levels than the current system does, "that doesn't mean you're going to have anywhere to put" inmates deemed a higher risk, he said.

In an October report, the MDOC said 641 inmates were classified as Level 5 and just over 4,000 as Level 4.

The MDOC in September announced plans to add 870 high-security beds. But Osborn said most of those beds won't be ready for years and corrections officers and inmates need action now.

Osborn said he's also concerned that the MDOC may be moving to a fully automated system that won't include the recommendations of corrections officers who deal with inmates on a daily basis. Not all of the information officers can provide about inmate behavior is necessarily found in reports that will be automatically inputted into the new system, he said.
